props.title: Casanova
props.initialSlug: The world's greatest lover meets his match

sections.content: Federico Fellini's **Casanova** (1976) represents the maestro's most lavish and grotesque carnival of excess, starring Donald Sutherland in an eerily mechanical performance as history's legendary lover. The film deliberately subverts the romantic myth of Casanova, presenting instead a hollow automaton moving through a series of increasingly bizarre sexual encounters. This approach shares DNA with Stanley Kubrick's Barry Lyndon (1975), another period piece that uses artificial stylization to comment on social performance, though Fellini pushes further into surrealism.

sections.content: The film's artificial aesthetic - with its obvious studio sets, theatrical lighting, and deliberately fake-looking costumes - creates a dreamlike unreality that mirrors Casanova's own emotional emptiness. This technique influenced later biographical films like Amadeus (1984) and **Marie Antoinette** (2006), which similarly use stylized artifice to comment on their historical subjects. Fellini's Casanova exists in a world of masks, both literal and metaphorical, suggesting that identity itself is a kind of performance.

The mechanical bird that appears throughout the film becomes a central metaphor for Casanova himself - an automated pleasure-seeker going through predetermined motions. This mechanical element influenced later films about sexuality and artificiality like Eyes Wide Shut (1999) and **The Duke of Burgundy** (2014), which similarly explore the ritualistic nature of desire. movies.title: Eyes Wide Shut
movies.slug: Kubrick's final film follows a doctor's surreal sexual odyssey through Manhattan's elite secret societies

sections.content: Fellini's maximalist approach to production design reaches its apex here, with Giuseppe Rotunno's cinematography capturing a parade of grotesque carnival masks, elaborate costumes, and theatrical sets that would influence films like **The Cook, the Thief, His Wife & Her Lover** (1989) and **Prospero's Books** (1991). The film's emphasis on artifice over realism established a template for stylized biographical films that prioritize impression over fact, seen in works like **I'm Not There** (2007) and **Velvet Goldmine** (1998).
